$comment: Rights the conduct violated, named beyond the enumerated constitutional catalogue. Each is tied to the instrument that recognises it, or marked unenumerated where no positive instrument does. IMPORTANT: most of these instruments postdate most of these entries and none applies retroactively. A right named here characterises the conduct, exactly as offense[] does; it is not an assertion that a remedy was available at the time. See METHODOLOGY.md, Rights beyond the enumerated catalogue.

rights.name: Life
instruments: U.S. Const. amends. V, XIV (due process)
rights.note: The most basic and, in this corpus, the most often violated with no consequence. Present in domestic law throughout; the failure was never one of recognition.

rights.name: Liberty and security of person
Freedom from slavery and servitude
rights.note: Domestically recognised only from 1865. For every entry before that date the conduct was lawful, which is a fact about the forum and not about the right.

rights.name: Freedom from torture and cruel treatment
Recognition everywhere as a person before the law
rights.note: The right Dred Scott denied by name. There is no domestic analogue stated this plainly, which is why the entry has no offence and no forum: the holding removed the capacity to complain of anything at all.

rights.name: Equality before the law
An effective remedy for acts violating fundamental rights
rights.note: The right this entire book is about. Every entry violates it by construction: an established act with no forum, no conviction and no restoration IS the denial of an effective remedy. It is therefore recorded on every entry and carries no information about any single one.

rights.name: Freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention
A fair and public hearing by an impartial tribunal
rights.note: Violated on the inverted track: the entries where the state prosecuted the people it had already injured.

rights.name: Freedom of movement and residence
rights.note: The right the displacement entries violate: banishment from Wilmington, expulsion from Ocoee, dispersal from Rosewood.

rights.name: To marry and to found a family; the family as the fundamental group unit of society
rights.note: Violated by sale in the trade entries and by operation in the sterilisation entry - once by separating a family and once by preventing one.

rights.name: To own property and not to be arbitrarily deprived of it
rights.note: No unqualified domestic analogue. Tulsa, Ocoee and Rosewood are the entries; in each the deprivation was permanent and the title moved.

rights.name: Freedom of opinion and expression, including to seek and impart information
To take part in government and to vote
Education
rights.note: No federal constitutional right to education exists domestically (San Antonio ISD v. Rodriguez, 411 U.S. 1 (1973)). The anti-literacy and Prince Edward entries violate a right recognised internationally and not domestically.

rights.name: To participate in cultural life, to enjoy the arts, and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits
rights.note: This is the instrument that names the right to create, to contribute, and to share in what a society produces. It is real positive international law and it is the closest existing recognition of the interest that the foreclosed_contribution field records. It has no domestic constitutional analogue.

rights.name: The highest attainable standard of physical and mental health
rights.note: The United States signed but has not ratified the ICESCR.

rights.name: Not to be subjected without free consent to medical or scientific experimentation
rights.note: Stated expressly in the ICCPR. The Tuskegee study ran for twenty-five years after the Nuremberg Code and the Relf sterilisations occurred while it was in force.

rights.name: Development: to participate in, contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development
instruments: UN Declaration on the Right to Development (1986), A/RES/41/128
rights.note: A declaration rather than a treaty, and the United States voted against it. Recorded here because it is the only instrument that names the interest in a people's own progress as a right.

rights.name: Reparation: restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction, and guarantees of non-repetition
instruments: UN Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy and Reparation (2005), A/RES/60/147
rights.note: The five forms map almost exactly onto restoration.forms in this book. Restitution and compensation are the two the corpus records as material; satisfaction is what it records as symbolic; guarantees of non-repetition are what it records as institutional reform. The mapping was not designed - the instrument and the log arrived at the same categories.

rights.name: To become what one might have become
rights.note: NO positive instrument recognises this. It is a moral claim, recorded here as one and marked so. It names the interest a person has in their own unrealised work - what they would have thought, made, built or discovered - and it is the interest that foreclosed_contribution records the destruction of. The nearest thing in law is UDHR art. 27, which protects participation in cultural and scientific life but does not reach the loss of a contribution never made because the contributor was killed. The book states this as a gap in the instruments, not as a right it can assert on anyone's behalf.
